title: Relaying through orbit
question: An aircraft flies 9,000 km from its gateway. Can a small satellite constellation keep the mesh connected?

headlines.label: of five orbits with a route to the aircraft
headlines.detail: six satellites in one plane; longest gap 19 min

headlines.label: with the same six satellites split across planes
headlines.detail: the inter-satellite ring only closes within one plane

headlines.label: deepest route the mesh found
headlines.detail: aircraft, satellites, gateway: routed hop by hop by BATMAN

summary: An aircraft flies out along a great circle, 7,648 km from its gateway by the end of the run, while the gateway tries to keep a route to it through a ring of satellites at 1,200 km, on real Keplerian orbits (109-minute period). Users can work a satellite only above 25° elevation, and the planet blocks any path that dips below its surface. The gateway has a workable satellite 49% of the time, but the aircraft is often under a different one thousands of kilometres away, so the traffic has to cross the ring between satellites. With six satellites in one plane the mesh keeps a route 36% of the time, as deep as 7 hops. Split the same six across planes and that falls to 24%: the links between neighbouring satellites only close inside a plane, so splitting them breaks exactly the hops the long route depends on.

charts.title: Constellation geometry: sky vs. reach
charts.caption: A route can exceed the gateway's own sky: the aircraft works a satellite the gateway cannot see, and the ring carries it home.

charts.title: Route depth vs. how far away the aircraft is (six in one plane)
charts.caption: Two hops is one satellite both ends can see. Three or more and the route is crossing the ring between satellites, which is what the far end of the flight depends on.

charts.title: Satellite passes over the gateway (first two hours)
charts.caption: Below 25° a user terminal will not work a satellite; each pass lasts minutes.

charts.title: How far away the aircraft is

method: Satellites follow circular Earth orbits rendered into a local east-north-up frame; the aircraft flies a great circle at 10 km and 250 m/s. User links are Ku-band (12 GHz) free-space loss at 66.7 dBm EIRP into a 35 dBi array, masked below 25° elevation and by the Earth itself. Inter-satellite links are a high-gain RF stand-in for optical links with an 8,000 km acquisition range. Every node runs the real wayfinder router with 2–10 s adverts, sampled every 5 s over five orbits per geometry.
